Infant drug discontinuation symptoms (e.g., irritability, low body temperature, uncontrollable crying, eating and sleeping disorders) were reported in about 10% of infants. One mother was taking 10 mg daily and 4 mothers were taking 20 mg daily. The most commonly reported adverse events in the infants were insomnia and restlessness; constant crying and poor feeding were less commonly reported. All of the adverse effects developed within the first 2 weeks after initiation of maternal treatment and disappeared within the 3 days after drug discontinuation. Adverse effects disappeared in one infant after reducing the maternal dosage from 20 mg daily to 10 mg daily. After paroxetine was begun, the mother reported severe constipation in the infant, which resolved within 2 days after discontinuing paroxetine with no treatment. No abnormalities were seen on physical examination or laboratory tests. The infant had previously developed agitation and sleeplessness with maternal sertraline use. The infant subsequently tolerated maternal citalopram use.[32] Five women were treated with paroxetine 7 to 25 mg daily during the third trimester of pregnancy and during breastfeeding. Pediatric evaluations including neurologic assessments and brain ultrasound were conducted during the first 24 hours postpartum. Further follow-up was conducted at 6 or more months of age. Infant clinical status was comparable to unexposed infants from the same pediatric department.[17] A case series reported 8 women who received paroxetine 20 mg and mirtazapine 15 mg daily for various psychiatric disorders. The women breastfed (extent not stated) their infants who averaged 4.3 weeks of age. The stools of infants exposed to an SSRI in milk had increases in the genera Gemella, Staphylococcus and Corynebacterium and a decrease in Lactobacillus.[36]

outputs.answer:
## What was actually observed in infants

- **Measured exposure:** Paroxetine was undetectable in infant serum in several studies, including 16 infants and pooled groups of 40 and 6 infants. Other studies detected low levels in some infants. Nondetection in a measured sample does not prove universal clinical safety. [S2](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501190/)
- **No apparent adverse effects in some groups:** Six infants had no clinically noted adverse reactions; a cohort of 15 infants had normal six-month weight gain and no abnormal effects reported; and some studies reported generally normal development. [S2](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501190/)
- **Reported symptoms:** Individual reports or small groups included agitation, difficulty feeding, irritability, sleepiness, constipation, insomnia, restlessness, crying, and poor feeding. Several reports involved exposure during pregnancy as well as breastfeeding, so the contribution of breastmilk exposure could not be determined. [S2](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501190/)
- **Developmental findings:** One study reported slight psychomotor delay in a small group, but the contribution of breastfeeding exposure could not be determined. Other follow-up studies reported normal or generally normal development. [S2](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501190/)
- **Case report:** One 18-month-old breastfed infant had vomiting, electrolyte abnormalities, and dehydration; paroxetine was detected but not quantified in the infant’s serum. The report considered paroxetine a possible cause, but strong evidence was lacking and other causes could not be excluded. The retrieved text states that the infant was thriving with a normal metabolic profile six weeks after breastfeeding was discontinued; it does not establish that paroxetine caused the abnormalities. [S2](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501190/)

## Recommendations to monitor

LactMed lists monitoring breastfed infants for **excess sedation, agitation, irritability, poor feeding, and poor weight gain**. These are recommendations, not observed outcomes in every infant and not evidence that the symptoms occurred simply because monitoring was advised. [S2](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501190/)

The retrieved LactMed record is explicitly **truncated**, so additional material may be missing from this lookup. [S2](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501190/)
